Work  /  FCSN — “I Count”
Campaign · Transit media · Multilingual

The hardest people to count are the ones who already feel invisible.

“I Count” ran across the MBTA in four languages in the spring of 2020, for families whose federal services depend on being counted — and who had every reason not to answer the door.

Client

Federation for Children with Special Needs

Services

Campaign concept, visual design, multilingual adaptation

Media

MBTA stations, Red & Orange lines, buses

Ran

4 May – 15 June 2020

Digital kiosk, transit concourse. Two words at walking speed.

The challenge

The census decides congressional representation and the allocation of federal funding. For families of children with disabilities, that is not an abstraction — the services they rely on are funded against the count. Children missed by the census are children the funding formula does not know exist.

The undercount is also self-reinforcing. The households least likely to respond are the ones that already feel unseen by government, which is precisely the group the campaign had to reach. And it ran May and June of 2020 — a pandemic spring, when a form from a federal agency was competing with far louder anxieties.

The medium made it harder still. Transit advertising gets seconds from a moving audience, in four languages — English, Spanish, Chinese and Haitian Creole — with no room to explain anything.

Station triptych: the stakes, the claim, the child. Read left to right at escalator speed.
Billboard. The same three moves, re-ordered for a horizontal format.

The approach

Two words, first person, present tense. “I Count” carries the whole argument. It states the civic fact — you are counted, the number matters — and the personal one underneath it, which is the reason the campaign existed at all. For a family used to their child being treated as an exception, the second reading is the one that lands.

It also survives the medium. Two words work at platform distance, on a moving bus, and in a language you did not design in. Anything requiring explanation would have failed on all three counts.

Four languages, one campaign. English, Spanish, Chinese and Haitian Creole. Translated slogans usually break — they lengthen, they lose the pun, they change register. A two-word first-person claim is about the only structure that survives intact, which is a design decision made at the naming stage rather than fixed in layout later.

Let the child make the claim. “Support Children Like Me. I Count.” — the first person is the child’s, not the viewer’s. Every photograph is a child looking straight out, smiling, at full size. Not a symbol of a category. A specific person who either gets counted or does not.

Four languages, four editions

English, Spanish, Haitian Creole and Chinese — each a full edition rather than a translated overlay, with its own photography, its own color and its own line. Yo cuento. Mwen Konte Tou. 我也算數。

The claim survives all four because it is two words in the first person. Nothing to translate but the grammar.

Haitian Creole — Mwen Konte Tou.
Spanish — Yo cuento.
Chinese — 我也算數。 Each language edition carries its own color, so the campaign reads as one family without any edition looking like a copy of another.

The outcome

Six weeks of paid transit media across Boston’s busiest lines, funded by a US Census Department grant distributed through the Massachusetts Secretary of State’s office.

The panels carried the stakes in plain numbers — “Help to determine hundreds of billions in federal funding” — alongside a QR code straight to the census form. Awareness and the action it needed, in the same frame.

Add participation or reach figures if FCSN or the Secretary of State published any.
